name: DATE

args.name: month
args.about: the month number, 1 to 12 (more rolls into the next year)

args.name: day
args.about: the day of the month (more rolls into the next month)

about: Makes a date from a year, a month and a day.

example.why: Year 2026, month 3, day 15 make 15 March 2026, shown as a date.

notes: Months and days past the end roll over: DATE(2026,14,1) is 1 February 2027.

name: DATEDIF

args.name: unit
args.about: "Y" whole years, "M" whole months, "D" days, or "YM", "YD", "MD" for what's left over

about: How many whole years, months or days lie between two dates.

example.why: From 20 June 1990 to 1 March 2026 is 35 whole years; the 36th birthday hasn't come yet.

notes: The start date must not be after the end date, or it gives #NUM!.

name: DATEVALUE

args.name: date_text
args.about: a date written as text, like "2026-03-15"

about: Turns a date written as text into a date number.

example.why: Dates are counted in days from 1 January 1900; 15 March 2026 is day 46096. Give the cell a date format to see it as a date.

name: DAY
about: The day of the month of a date, 1 to 31.

example.why: 15 March 2026 is the 15th day of the month.

name: EDATE

args.name: months
args.about: how many months later (negative for earlier)

about: The same day a number of months before or after a date.

example.why: One month after 31 January is 28 February 2026, as February has no 31st; it shows as the day number 46081 until the cell gets a date format.

name: EOMONTH

args.name: months
args.about: how many months later (0 for the same month, negative for earlier)

about: The last day of the month, a number of months before or after a date.

example.why: The last day of February 2026 is the 28th, day number 46081; give the cell a date format to see it as a date.

name: MONTH
about: The month of a date, 1 to 12.

example.why: March is the third month.

name: TIME
about: Makes a time of day from hours, minutes and seconds.

example.why: A time is a part of a day: 6 in the evening is three quarters of the way through it.

name: TIMEVALUE

args.name: time_text
args.about: a time written as text, like "14:30"

about: Turns a time written as text into a part of a day.

example.why: Midday is half of a day.

name: HOUR

args.name: time
args.about: a time or a date with a time

about: The hour of a time, 0 to 23.

example.why: 14:35 is in the 14th hour, 2 in the afternoon.

name: MINUTE

args.name: time
args.about: a time or a date with a time

about: The minutes of a time, 0 to 59.

example.why: 14:35:20 is 35 minutes past 2.

name: SECOND

args.name: time
args.about: a time or a date with a time

about: The seconds of a time, 0 to 59.

example.why: 14:35:20 has 20 seconds.

name: NOW
about: The date and time right now.

example.why: It changes every time the sheet works itself out again.

notes: TODAY gives the date without the time.

name: TODAY
about: Today's date.

example.why: It changes every day.

notes: NOW gives the time as well.

name: YEAR
about: The year of a date.

example.why: 15 March 2026 is in 2026.

name: NETWORKDAYS
about: How many working days (Monday to Friday) lie between two dates, counting both ends.

example.why: Two weeks from Monday 2 March to Friday 13 March have 10 weekdays; the holiday on 9 March leaves 9.

notes: NETWORKDAYS.INTL lets you say which days are the weekend.

name: NETWORKDAYS.INTL

args.name: weekend
args.about: which days are off: 1 Sat–Sun, 2 Sun–Mon… 11 Sunday only, or text like "0000011"

about: How many working days lie between two dates, with the weekend days you choose.

example.why: Weekend 11 means only Sunday is off: the 14 days from 2 to 15 March hold two Sundays, leaving 12.

name: DAYS
about: How many days lie between two dates.

example.why: From 2 March to 20 March is 18 days. The later date comes first.

name: DAYS360

args.name: method
args.about: FALSE for the US way (the usual), TRUE for the European way

about: How many days lie between two dates, counting every month as 30 days, as some accounts do.

example.why: Two months of 30 days each make 60, though the calendar has 59 days between them.

name: WEEKDAY

args.name: return_type
args.about: 1 for Sunday=1…Saturday=7 (the usual), 2 for Monday=1…Sunday=7, 3 for Monday=0…Sunday=6

about: Which day of the week a date falls on, as a number.

example.why: 18 March 2026 is a Wednesday, the third day when Monday is 1.

name: WEEKNUM

args.name: return_type
args.about: 1 if weeks start on Sunday (the usual), 2 if they start on Monday

about: Which week of the year a date is in, counting the week with 1 January as week 1.

example.why: Week 1 is 1–3 January (weeks start on Sunday), and Sunday 15 March starts week 12.

notes: ISOWEEKNUM gives the week numbers used in Europe, where week 1 is the first with a Thursday.

name: WORKDAY

args.name: days
args.about: how many working days later (negative for earlier)

about: The date a number of working days (Monday to Friday) after a date.

example.why: Five working days after Friday 6 March skip the weekend and land on Friday 13 March, day number 46094.

notes: WORKDAY.INTL lets you say which days are the weekend.

name: WORKDAY.INTL

args.name: days
args.about: how many working days later (negative for earlier)

args.name: weekend
args.about: which days are off: 1 Sat–Sun, 7 Fri–Sat, 11 Sunday only… or text like "0000011"

about: The date a number of working days after a date, with the weekend days you choose.

example.why: With only Sunday off, five working days after Friday 6 March are Sat 7, Mon 9, Tue 10, Wed 11 and Thu 12 March (day number 46093).

name: YEARFRAC

args.name: basis
args.about: how days are counted: 0 US 30/360 (the usual), 1 actual days, 2 actual/360, 3 actual/365, 4 European 30/360

about: What part of a year lies between two dates.

example.why: Six months of 30 days are 180 of the 360 days in a year this way of counting.

name: ISOWEEKNUM
about: The ISO week number of a date, the one used on calendars in Europe.

example.why: ISO weeks start on Monday and week 1 is the one with the year's first Thursday (1 January 2026 is a Thursday), so 18 March is in week 12.
